item.title: Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles
item.description:
If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

item.title: Did voters disregard politics and feel they just couldn’t stand Trump ?
item.description:
Hee’s a quick take on the election.

It’s been interesting and sometimes comical watching people explaining the election results with excuses, analyses, rationalizations, anger, finger pointing, and hindsight.

Inflation, war with Iran, corruption, and ICE tactics have been cited as reasons why the Donald Trump presidency and the MAGA ideas were so soundly rejected.

Those things, large and small, were all part of it -  but perhaps there was also something else at play.

For those on the fence over the issues and the state of the nation, maybe one conspicuous thing could have been what pushed them over the edge:

Trump is just plain unlikable.

He is seen as cruel, vindictive, corrupt, thin skinned, and egotistical beyond the scope of the word. And he lies as easily as he breathes.

Did some voters disregard politics and finally feel they just couldn’t stand him anymore?

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

item.title: Refineries are rethinking what they produce
item.description:
A new analysis from the federal Energy Information Administration shows that this year, oil refineries in the U.S. have been shifting some of their production capacity away from gasoline. They’re producing more “middle distillates,” which includes jet fuel and diesel. The global supply of those products has been tight. item.title: Teaching financial advisors the depth behind tools and recipes
item.description:
When you cook, do you follow a recipe precisely or adapt it as you go? My wife uses the second approach. She will make something extraordinary, and when I ask if she wrote down what she did, she has no idea. She tasted, adjusted, and added a little of this or that. I am the opposite. Give me a recipe, and I’m fine; just don’t ask me to be creative.

That’s probably why, in my long-ago first sales job in real estate, I initially relied on the decision tree the manager gave me. “If the client says this, go here. If they object, go there.” I tried to memorize every branch. If a customer said something that wasn’t on any of them, I had nothing.

You have probably sat across from someone like that, maybe an insurance agent reading from a script or a financial advisor going through a standard questionnaire without looking up. You can feel the difference when someone is rigidly following a recipe rather than listening to you and responding to your needs and concerns.

The difference matters when someone is handling your financial life. Most advisor training works tool-first. You learn the exercise, practice it, and repeat it until you know the recipe and master the skill.

Breanna Blaney, founder of the Anya Institute and creator of the Integrative Wealth Advisor certification, uses a different approach to train financial advisors. Before her students learn any client-facing tools, they spend months doing their own inner work, examining their own relationship with money and their own blind spots. Only then do they learn the techniques. “I teach people how to cook,” she says, “not what the recipe is.”

When I introduce the emotional side of money to my financial planning students at Golden Gate University, the most common reaction is shock that it was never part of their formal education. “This is hard,” they say when I ask them to sit quietly with their own thoughts for a few minutes. If it is that hard for them, imagine how difficult it is for a planner without that practice to guide clients through their money issues.

Jacob Moreno, the founder of psychodrama, used the phrase “getting on the balcony” to describe rising above the action to observe what is actually happening rather than reacting. A financial advisor on the balcony asks better questions, notices what you are not saying, and does not flinch when the conversation moves past the numbers. Blaney’s description for this is, “I’m looking at you. I’m seeing you first.”

In practice, that means the advisor does not default to running you through the same sequence of questions, exercises, or rote processes they use with every client. They will not rush past the emotion to get to the spreadsheet. If you need to talk about why you cannot bring yourself to sell your late parents’ house before you can discuss the tax implications, an advisor who has done their own work will follow you there.

If you are looking for a financial advisor, here are some clues that someone knows how to cook rather than just how to follow a recipe:

  1. They ask about your life before they ask about your portfolio.

  2. They listen and clarify before they offer advice.

  3. They can sit with a difficult subject without changing it.

  4. They have examined their own relationship with money before trying to guide yours.

For a financial advisor, having a recipe book of skills and processes is essential. Just as important is knowing when and how to tweak those recipes to give clients the service and support they need.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

item.title: Tesla to end Cybertruck production as sales stall at ~10% of plan
item.description:
Tesla is ending Cybertruck production. CEO Elon Musk announced early Friday that the automaker will “wind down” the electric pickup at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, about three and a half years after the first deliveries.

Musk says it’s to make room for more Cybercab production. But Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck is short on buyers, and it sells at roughly a tenth of the 250,000 units a year Tesla built its line for.

item.title: Data centers lost in the midterms
item.description:
Voters have made their dissatisfaction quite clear with the tech status quo. And it sounds like the Democrats gearing up to take power in the House and Senate might actually do something about that.


Plus, Big Tech spent big on races in this election, but didn't get a whole lot of bang for their buck. But first, a tech issue that was actually on the ballot: data centers. More than 40 jurisdictions across 10 states voted to put them on ice. However, Harwood, North Dakota, gave them the green light. Paresh Dave, senior writer at Wired, joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino to explain more about all this on this week’s “Tech Bytes: Week in Review.”


More on this:


“America got the anti-data-center wave it voted for. Here come the economic consequences” from CNN

item.title: ChatGPT for Teens' safeguards don't work, risk assessment finds
item.description:
OpenAI's new teen-appropriate version of ChatGPT may not be living up to its promises, according to an independent evaluation. The new mode is supposed to have stronger guardrails for sensitive topics, automatic parental alerts and a study tool that won't just give kids the answers to their homework.


But the nonprofit Common Sense Media evaluated the tool and found it poses "unacceptable risks." Tom Siegel leads the Youth Safety Institute at Common Sense and tested about 4,000 prompts using fake teen accounts. He spoke with Meghan McCarty Carino about his findings.


More on this:


“ChatGPT for Teens Poses Unacceptable Risk to Kids, Common Sense Media Finds” from Common Sense Media

item.title: Farmers need help. Let’s see if a Dem-led congress can provide it
item.description:
Though grain and soybean prices have come up a bit in recent months, the American Farm Bureau thinks that farmers will continue to see tough times. Prices for their crops just aren’t  keeping up with input costs, principally fertilizer and diesel fuel. 

So far, the Trump administration’s policies haven’t been able to make much of a difference by way of financial relief, so the White House turned to making direct cash payments to farmers in order for many of them to stay afloat.

Much as I support federal financial aid in order to keep producers functioning – food security is priority number one – an efficiently structured relationship between farmers and policy-makers in Washington is what the ag industry needs.

The Trump administration has been helpless when it comes to framing policy that works for farmers, which makes cash bailouts a necessity and only extends official ineptitude.  

Last night’s overwhelming rejection of Trump and his policies was driven in large part by rural states that turned on the president’s party. Though South Dakota didn’t participate in the political overhaul, farmers in our state will be impacted by the changes in ag policies that should materialize in D.C. next year.  

The first order of business should be passing a Farm Bill. Agriculture is a high risk business, subjected to sometimes wild price fluctuations and the vagaries of weather. Farm bills provide safety nets that farmers and their lenders can depend on. 

Farmers also need an administration that knows something about how trade policy can affect rural livelihoods. Trump’s wild and irrational trade wars have permanently altered the soybean market, and not for the better as far as American producers are concerned.

Now that Democrats from rural areas are part of the political landscape in D.C. we should expect better when it comes to dealing with the headstrong Trump, who up to now had a Republican congress green-lighting policies that drove crop prices down and pushed input prices up.

Will the Democrats perform? I think they will, especially as much of their newfound political strength comes from the rural districts that terminated their Republican reps yesterday. 

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission. 

Photo: South Dakota farm, public domain, wikimedia commons

If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.
item.source:markdown:
Though grain and soybean prices have come up a bit in recent months, the [American Farm Bureau](https://www.fb.org/news-release/farmer-losses-projected-to-deepen) thinks that farmers will continue to see tough times. Prices for their crops just aren’t keeping up with input costs, principally fertilizer and diesel fuel.
So far, the Trump administration’s policies haven’t been able to make much of a difference by way of financial relief, so the White House turned to making [direct cash payments](https://www.usda.gov/about-usda/news/press-releases/2026/10/19/trump-administration-announces-8-billion-harvest-fuel-relief-program) to farmers in order for many of them to stay afloat.
Much as I support federal financial aid in order to keep producers functioning – food security is priority number one – an efficiently structured relationship between farmers and policy-makers in Washington is what the ag industry needs.
The Trump administration has been helpless when it comes to framing policy that works for farmers, which makes cash bailouts a necessity and only extends official ineptitude.
Last night’s overwhelming rejection of Trump and his policies was driven in large part by [rural states](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/how-democrats-expanded-map-won-rural-america-2026-11-04/) that turned on the president’s party. Though [South Dakota didn’t participate](https://www.google.com/search?q=electoral+map+south+dakota+2026&rlz=1CAEVJI_enUS997US997&oq=electoral+map+south+dakota+2026&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigATIHCAIQIRigATIHCAMQIRigATIHCAQQIRigATIHCAUQIRigAdIBCTEwOTk4ajBqNKgCA7ACAfEFEBGNsM8cbes&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) in the political overhaul, farmers in our state will be impacted by the changes in ag policies that should materialize in D.C. next year.
The first order of business should be [passing a Farm Bill](https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/who-we-are/how-we-work/policy/supporting-the-farm-bill/). Agriculture is a high risk business, subjected to sometimes wild price fluctuations and the vagaries of weather. Farm bills provide safety nets that farmers and their lenders can depend on.
Farmers also need an administration that knows something about how trade policy can affect rural livelihoods. Trump’s wild and irrational trade wars have [permanently altered the soybean market](https://www.investopedia.com/soybean-exports-to-china-are-gone-and-may-never-fully-recover-11835118), and not for the better as far as [American producers](https://www.cato.org/blog/trumps-trade-wars-harm-farmers-taxpayers) are concerned.
Now that Democrats from rural areas are part of the political landscape in D.C. we should expect better when it comes to dealing with the headstrong Trump, who up to now had a Republican congress [green-lighting](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/26/donald-trump-policy-disaster-rural-america) policies that [drove crop prices down](https://www.cato.org/blog/trumps-trade-wars-harm-farmers-taxpayers) and [pushed input prices up](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/08/25/farmers-say-they-face-new-crisis-trumps-tariffs-iran-war-raise-costs/).
Will the Democrats perform? I think they will, especially as much of their newfound political strength comes from the rural districts that terminated their Republican reps yesterday.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. item.title: Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined
item.description:
Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

item.title: Tesla accused of selling FSD to Korean owners who can’t legally use it
item.description:
A South Korean consumer group is asking regulators to stop Tesla from marketing “Full Self-Driving” to customers whose cars can’t legally run it. By Tesla’s own numbers, that covers 99% of the Teslas it sold in Korea last year.

Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty plans to file the complaint with the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) on Thursday, according to Reuters, which reviewed it. It comes just a week after a Seoul court threw out a refund lawsuit from Korean owners who paid for FSD.

item.title: Song sung blue? No. Last night was the Hallelujah Chorus sung blue
item.description:
Last night’s rebuke of Donald Trump should be a long-needed slap in the GOP’s collective face. His party has needed to come out of its Trump-induced stupor for a long time. 

Trump caused this because he has taken the Republican Party on a path that has veered away from long-standing conservative principles, creating problems that led to a sweeping rejection of him and his loyalists.

If Trump had been true to Republican principles, this wouldn’t have happened.  

  • If Trump had followed traditional GOP practice and ideology, his tariff binge would not have occurred. Republicans have historically been champions of free trade. During the Reagan and Bush era, free trade initiatives, particularly the development of the World Trade Organization, were a top priority. Back in 2017, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds was writing about the benefits of trade agreements and their importance to South Dakota. Trump’s tariff agenda has been bad for South Dakota and the country in  general, particularly on the inflation front.

  • Trump’s rhetoric on immigration completely reversed the attitude that was prevalent during the Reagan-Bush era. Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric and policies have had a negative effect on the economy.

  • Trump’s energy policies, which lead to greater dependence on fossil fuels, have been a disaster. “Drill, baby, drill” is about the dumbest approach to energy management I can think of, and I think about it every time I have to shell out serious bucks for a tankful of gasoline.  George W. Bush was a strong supporter of renewable energy.  Why Trump won’t follow suit is a mystery. 

The common denominator for the way Trump has turned away from policies common to his recent Republican predecessors in the White House is inflation – and clearly, inflation is one of the main causes of the discontent that led to last night’s debacle. Trump has created an identity crisis for his party, and the public has just shown that it has had enough of it.

Hallelujah.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
Last night’s rebuke of Donald Trump should be a long-needed slap in the GOP’s collective face. His party has needed to come out of its Trump-induced stupor for a long time.
Trump caused this because he has taken the Republican Party on a path that has veered away from long-standing conservative principles, creating problems that led to a sweeping rejection of him and his loyalists.
If Trump had been true to Republican principles, this wouldn’t have happened.
- If Trump had followed [traditional GOP practice and ideology](https://abcnews.com/Business/past-republican-presidents-tariffs/story?id=116268942), his tariff binge would not have occurred. Republicans have historically been champions of free trade. During the Reagan and Bush era, free trade initiatives, particularly the development of the World Trade Organization, were a top priority. [Back in 2017](https://www.rounds.senate.gov/newsroom/weekly-column/trade-agreements-vital-to-south-dakotas-economy), South Dakota senator Mike Rounds was writing about the benefits of trade agreements and their importance to South Dakota. Trump’s tariff agenda has been [bad for South Dakota](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2025/05/27/south-dakota-governors-economic-advisers-bemoan-trumps-tariff-policy/) and the country in general, [particularly on the inflation front](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/tracking-economic-effects-tariffs).
- Trump’s [rhetoric on immigration](https://theconversation.com/republicans-once-championed-immigration-in-the-us-why-has-the-partys-rhetoric-and-public-opinion-changed-so-dramatically-239836) completely reversed the attitude that was prevalent during the Reagan-Bush era. Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric and policies have had a [negative effect](https://equitablegrowth.org/economic-research-shows-immigration-is-good-for-u-s-workers-the-economy-and-affordability/) on the economy.
- Trump’s [energy policies](https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/inflation-numbers-show-trump-administration-energy-policies-infecting-nations), which lead to greater dependence on fossil fuels, have been a disaster. [“Drill, baby, drill”](https://www.google.com/search?q=drill+baby+drill+trump&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=drill+baby+drill&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUqDAgBEAAYFBiHAhiABDIGCAAQRRg5MgwIARAAGBQYhwIYgAQyBwgCEAAYgAQyBwgDEAAYgAQyBwgEEAAYgAQyBwgFEAAYgAQyCggGEAAYgAQYtAcyBwgHEAAYgAQyBwgIEAAYgAQyBwgJEAAYgATSAQg3NjI1ajBqN6gCALACAA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) is about the dumbest approach to energy management I can think of, and I think about it every time I have to shell out serious bucks for a tankful of gasoline. [George W. Bush was a strong supporter](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-president-bush-signs-into-law-national-energy-plan) of renewable energy. Why Trump won’t follow suit is a mystery.
The common denominator for the way Trump has turned away from policies common to his recent Republican predecessors in the White House is [inflation](https://fortune.com/2025/08/16/trump-deportation-immigration-inflation-2026/) – and clearly, inflation is one of the main causes of the discontent that led to last night’s debacle. Trump has created an identity crisis for his party, and the public has just shown that it has had enough of it.
Hallelujah.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Data centers were on the ballot. They lost.
item.description:
Voter frustration with the economy helped the Democrats win control of Congress. But data centers were also on the ballot yesterday, and they got a big thumbs down from voters. Voters were deciding on more than 40 data center measures. According to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot, voters passed 33 provisions to restrict data centers. Only one proposal to allow more data centers passed. Plus, the day after midterms, how should you navigate political conversations at work?

item.title: The promise and risks of AI for mental health support
item.description:
This story includes references to suicide, self-harm and mental health crises. If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Available 24/7.


A growing number of lawsuits accuse AI companies of harming users — alleging chatbots have encouraged self-harm, reinforced delusions, or failed to recognize signs of distress.


And yet at the same time, a growing number of users, particularly younger ones, say they're turning to AI for emotional support.


Dr. John Torous studies how technology interacts with mental health. He says in the case of AI, it's complicated.


More on this:


Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows — from NPR


An independent benchmark for AI in mental health — from MindBench.ai


Development, validation and AI chatbot evaluation of the Adolescent Mental Health AI Response Tool — from Nature
item.source:markdown:
**_This story includes references to suicide, self-harm and mental health crises. If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call or text 988 to reach the_** **_[Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/)_** **_. Available 24/7._**
A growing number of [lawsuits](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-chatbots-serious-psychological-harms) accuse AI companies of harming users — alleging chatbots have encouraged self-harm, reinforced delusions, or failed to recognize signs of distress.
And yet at the same time, a growing number of users, particularly younger ones, [say they're turning to AI for emotional support.](https://www.rand.org/news/press/2026/06/nearly-1-in-5-us-adolescents-and-young-adults-use-ai.html)
Dr. John Torous studies how technology interacts with mental health. He says in the case of AI, it's complicated.
_More on this:_
[Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/30/nx-s1-6022278/ai-artificial-intelligence-teens-jed-common-sense-media) — from NPR
[An independent benchmark for AI in mental health](https://mindbench.ai/) — from MindBench.ai

item.title: When it comes to the job market, love the one you're with
item.description:
The September Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey from the BLS is out, and things in this labor market are mostly unchanged, although quits were up a bit. Still, economists are clear: Now is not the time to leave your job without another one lined up. Also in this episode: That stiff labor market may be hampering productivity, warehousing costs are up as retailers scramble for the holidays, and pro baseball faces a lockout in 2027.


Every story has an economic angle. Want some in your inbox? Subscribe to our daily or weekly newsletter.

  • Quits ticked up in September, but economists say it’s still a terrible time to leave your job
  • Sometimes leaving the workforce turns into a labor of love
  • Why warehouse space is getting harder and more expensive to come by

item.title: Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe
item.description:
Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

item.source:markdown:

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.
The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

item.title: Why so many men are opting out of the workforce
item.description:
It’s a big week for labor market data, including data on wages, unemployment, and job turnover. But before the employment floodgates open, it’s worth looking at a group of workers who have stepped back from the labor force: Men ages 25 to 54 — who were almost all working half a century ago — are participating significantly less today. What gives? Also: a look at how the U.S. trade balance is holding up.

item.title: Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay
item.description:
Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

more…

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. item.title: What are tokenized stocks?
item.description:
Back in September, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission cleared the way for the trading of tokenized stocks. The so-called “Innovation Exemption” temporarily lifts some regulations to allow for the issuance of digital tokens, which represent shares in a corporation or organization. In other words, it’s another way for investors to trade. This morning, we explain it all. But first, Marriott’s earnings beat expectations, even as some customers tighten their belts.

item.title: How Dick Nixon tried to kill South Dakota Senator Karl Mundt
item.description:
Author’s note: The difference between a memoir and an autobiography is that a memoir tells the story as best the author can remember it.  An autobiography has to be fact-checked.  This falls into the category of mini-memoir.  

As a young speech and social studies instructor at Eastern State Normal School in the 1930s in Madison, South Dakota, once upon a time a teacher college that is now known as Dakota State University, Karl Mundt developed a name for two reasons. He founded the National Forensics League, a speech and debate organization for high school students nationwide. He traveled around eastern South Dakota demonstrating his skill as a public speaker.  Soon the idea arose that it might be good if someday he might run for Congress. Since the Board of Regents could not abide political campaigning by its employees, Mundt was summoned to the Dean’s office.

You are an outstanding speech instructor, the Dean supposedly told him, and I do not want to lose you, but as a possible political candidate you cannot have a contract to teach here. “I do not need a contract,” Mundt replied. “I shall be happy to continue teaching, but if after two weeks there is no pay envelope in my mailbox, my enthusiasm for teaching will wane considerably.”

In 1938 he won a seat in Congress, then later the Senate. He was on the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he taught young California Congressman Richard Nixon how to hunt Commies. In 1954 Mundt chaired the Army-McCarthy hearings.  He rose to become second-ranking Republican on the Appropriations Committee and delivered a fair amount of pork to South Dakota.  

In 1969 he suffered a major stroke. His wife Mary, whom he met and married at University, believed he would recover and rebuffed efforts to have Karl step aside. As 1970 dawned it became clear that a Democrat might defeat Governor Frank Farrar and win the Governorship, and with it the ability to appoint a replacement to Mundt if he should die in office. Republican leaders wanted him to resign so Republican Farrar could appoint a replacement before the Democrats took the Governor’s Mansion. 

First a hometown delegation of Republicans appeared at the door to Mundt’s home on Capitol Hill. Mary fussed in the kitchen and made coffee for them. We must protect this seat for the GOP, they argued.  Karl deserves to enjoy well-earned retirement. Mary scolded them for being disloyal.  

Next a delegation of statewide Republican leaders knocked on the door.  A gracious welcome, but same thing. Shame on you, she said. 

South Dakota’s Republican Governor Frank Farrar also tried, but that had no chance. Farrar had been floating the idea of running against Karl in the 1972 Republican primary. Mary adamantly opposed Karl’s resigning if it meant Farrar might appoint himself to the Senate seat.  

Not long after that a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt residence.  Out came the President of the United States, Richard M. Nixon. He walked to the door and knocked. Mary welcomed him in. “Oh, Mr. President, Karl will be so happy to see you.” Mundt was sitting on a couch and may have been cognizant but, because of his stroke, was unable to string words together — a horrible loss for such a powerful orator. 

While Mary was in the kitchen fussing to make coffee, the Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces turned to the young Naval orderly who was helping care for the Senator. Nixon pointed to cigar boxes on the top shelf of a bookcase. “What are those?” he asked. 

“We have to constantly hide cigars from the Senator,” was the reply. “The doctor says if he smokes another he will have a big stroke and die."

Thereafter, once a week a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt home and a representative of the White House personally handed the Senator a box of cigars from President Nixon.

Jody Severson is a retired political and marketing consultant whose first campaign was "Clean for Gene" McCarthy in 1968.  He was a consultant in scores of campaigns at the statewide, local, and national levels from the north woods of Minnesota to the bayous of Louisiana. A native of Madison, SD, he has lived in Rapid City since the 1980s. 

Photo: Then U.S. Representative Karl Mundt, 1940, public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

item.title: Behind the scenes of an abandoned cyber-scam compound
item.description:

Reporter Leila Goldstein takes us behind the scenes of an abandoned scam compound in southeast Cambodia.

In many cases, it’s not just one bad actor but an entire network of scammers. And Cambodia has become a major hub for the industry. Last year, the U.S. issued [more than 100 sanctions](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0278) tied to fraud operations in the country.

item.title: Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls
item.description:
Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

item.title: Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear
item.description:
The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

item.title: My wish list if there is a blue wave in tomorrow’s election
item.description:
If the Democrats take Congress tomorrow, fixing Trump’s mess should be the first item on the legislative agenda.

From an ag-oriented South Dakotan’s perspective, I want to see Congress undo the president’s tariffs.  It has the power to do so. They’ve been such a drag on our country’s farm economy that getting rid of them will loosen up long-standing supply chain disruptions and get some liquidity back into the world’s distribution networks.

Congress should use all the tools at its disposal to get Trump to end his useless war in Iran. Its inflationary impact and waste of lives and money need to cease.

Problems of affordability have to be addressed, and they will be if tariffs are rescinded and the Iran war comes to a close. More broadly, Congress can address the affordability crisis through legislative actions aimed at housing supply, tax policy, and health care costs.

Given the way climate change is accelerating, we need more in in the way of green energy incentives and fossil fuel regulation.

Immigration policy should be focused on getting undocumented but otherwise law-abiding immigrants on the pathways to legalization. This was Ronald Reagan’s approach, and it worked. Trump’s policy of rounding them up and deporting them wholesale amounts to a deplorable lack of humanity. If you have a Judeo-Christian bent, read Leviticus 19:33-34. If you’re focused on the practical, economic consequences of Trump’s heavy-handed policy, consider that it’s causing a labor shortage in this country.

The list is long and complex, but a resounding political mandate tomorrow will at least make it approachable.

Let’s get out there and vote.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.
item.source:markdown:
If the Democrats take Congress tomorrow, fixing Trump’s mess should be the first item on the legislative agenda.
_From an ag-oriented South Dakotan’s perspective_, I want to see Congress undo the president’s tariffs. It [has the power](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/can-congress-reverse-trump's-tariffs) to do so. They’ve been such a [drag on our country’s farm economy](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/already-under-financial-pressure-farmers-squeezed-further-by-tariffs-and-iran-war) that getting rid of them will loosen up long-standing [supply chain disruptions](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/institute/articles/tariffs-stressing-manufacturers-supply-chains) and [get some liquidity](https://www.farmaid.org/blog/what-tariffs-mean-for-american-farmers/) back into the world’s distribution networks.
_Congress should_ [_use all the tools_](https://globalaffairs.org/commentary/analysis/can-new-congress-compel-trump-end-iran-war) _at its disposal_ to get Trump to end his useless war in Iran. Its [inflationary impact](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/13/economy/iran-war-oil-gas-prices-inflation) and waste of lives and money need to cease.
_Problems of affordability_ have to be addressed, and they will be if tariffs are rescinded and the Iran war comes to a close. More broadly, [Congress can address](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13189) the affordability crisis through legislative actions aimed at housing supply, tax policy, and health care costs.
_Given the way climate change is_ [_accelerating_](https://e360.yale.edu/digest/warming-gaining-pace), we need more in in the way of green energy incentives and fossil fuel regulation.
_Immigration policy_ should be focused on getting undocumented but otherwise law-abiding immigrants on the pathways to legalization. This was [Ronald Reagan’s approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_Reform_and_Control_Act_of_1986), and it worked. [Trump’s policy](https://www.cfr.org/articles/ice-and-deportations-how-trump-reshaping-immigration-enforcement) of rounding them up and deporting them wholesale amounts to a deplorable lack of humanity. If you have a Judeo-Christian bent, read [Leviticus 19:33-34](https://www.bible.com/bible/111/LEV.19.33-34.NIV). If you’re focused on the practical, economic consequences of Trump’s heavy-handed policy, consider that it’s [causing a labor shortage](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jul/29/trump-immigration-crackdown-labor-shortages-slowdowns) in this country.
The list is long and complex, but a resounding political mandate tomorrow will at least make it approachable.
Let’s get out there and vote.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: What it means when AI helps solve complex math problems
item.description:
In September, OpenAI said that its models had solved one of math's famous Millennium Prize problems. Then, the lab dropped more than 700 papers tackling another 400 complex problems with more breakthroughs to come.


These developments have caused something of an existential crisis in the math world. But Alex Kontorovich, a professor of math at Rutgers University, says they're a gift.

item.title: How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes
item.description:
Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

item.title: We have a winner in the Iran war, and the winner is …
item.description:
… the oil industry and its shareholders. Glancing across yesterday’s earning reports on the financial sites, the first headline I encountered in The Wall Street Journal announced “American Oil Giants See Profits Soar as Wars Crimp Energy Supplies.” The sub-head? “ExxonMobil and Chevron post blockbuster earnings for third quarter as world turns to U.S. refineries for fuel.” 

ExxonMobil’s profits doubled compared to the same period last year. Chevron’s were up 185%. Meantime, we consumers are gagging at our local gas pumps, paying an average of $4.12/gallon, about a buck over what we were paying a year ago.

This is what Donald Trump has wrought. 

Though he has since claimed that he was misinterpreted, Trump at the onset of the war said that it would be over in a matter of weeks. Since then the timeline has shifted. The last I heard, he said the war will end “soon,” a comfortably meaningless word when it comes to specificty. That and his claims of being misunderstood only amplify his incoherence on the subject.

That Trump recently said “we’re in the golden age of America … our nation is doing better now than ever before” only amplifies his detachment from reality.

Meanwhile, as the back and forth on what-Trump-said vs. what-Trump-meant goes on, the practical effect of Trump’s invasion of Iran has been to make oil producers much, much richer and helpless oil consumers all the poorer.

As to the president trying to do something about high fuel costs, Trump has come up way short. His feeble efforts to ease diesel fuel prices by engineering a deal that would let Russia increase diesel fuel exports were a fantasy (Foreign Policy calls the deal a “hail Mary”) from the get-go. Not only have diesel prices not gone down, they’ve actually risen by 7 cents/gallon since the deal was announced.

On the gasoline front, Trump’s only utterances about potentially lower prices are that gas will get cheaper once the Iran war ends. That stands to reason, but the price-dropping process will be slow-going once the Strait of Hormuz opens."If and when that happens, it will be a very long, multi-month to multi-year process for things to fully normalize,"  says a GasBuddy petroleum expert quoted on CBS.

The economically painful results of Trump’s hapless venture into the Persian Gulf will linger for a long time. The Center for Strategic and International Studies sees localized conflicts, many of them stirred up during Trump’s incursion into the area, as a “postwar threat to Gulf energy infrastructure.”

Unclear as Trump’s objectives in this war have been, his options seem even more muddled, which is a natural follow-up to the discordant statements and erratic strategies that got us into this mess in the first place.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and comm,entary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Glancing across yesterday’s earning reports on the financial sites, the first headline I encountered in [The Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/exxonmobil-xom-chevron-cvx-3q-earnings-report-2026-stock-1d890682) announced “American Oil Giants See Profits Soar as Wars Crimp Energy Supplies.” The sub-head? “ExxonMobil and Chevron post blockbuster earnings for third quarter as world turns to U.S. refineries for fuel.”
ExxonMobil’s profits doubled compared to the same period last year. Chevron’s were up 185%. Meantime, we consumers are gagging at our local gas pumps, [paying](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/30/business/big-oil-profits-trump-gas-prices) an average of $4.12/gallon, about a buck over what we were paying a year ago.
This is what Donald Trump has wrought.
Though he has [since claimed](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/02/politics/fact-check-trump-iran-timeline) that he was misinterpreted, Trump at the onset of the war said that it would be over in a matter of weeks. Since then [the timeline has shifted](https://politifact.com/article/2026/mar/30/trump-hegseth-iran-war-timeline/). The last I heard, he said the [war will end “soon](https://www.cbsnews.com/us-iran-tensions/),” a comfortably meaningless word when it comes to specificty. That and his claims of being misunderstood only amplify his [incoherence](https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026/oct/08/seth-meyers-jimmy-kimmel-trump-iran-camp-david) on the subject.
That Trump [recently said](https://“We’re in the golden age of America. So our nation is doing better now than ever before,”) “we’re in the golden age of America … our nation is doing better now than ever before” only amplifies his detachment from reality.
Meanwhile, as the back and forth on what-Trump-said vs. what-Trump-meant goes on, the practical effect of Trump’s invasion of Iran has been to make oil producers much, much richer and helpless oil consumers all the poorer.
As to the president trying to do something about high fuel costs, Trump has come up way short. His feeble efforts to ease diesel fuel prices by engineering a deal that would let Russia increase diesel fuel exports were a [fantasy](https://www.sdstandardnow.com/home/trumps-deal-on-russian-diesel-fuel-isnt-likely-to-lower-fuel-prices-for-farmers) ( [Foreign Policy](https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/30/trump-russia-diesel-deal-putin-prices-midterms-iran-war/) calls the deal a “hail Mary”) from the get-go. Not only have diesel prices not gone down, they’ve actually [risen by 7 cents/gallon](https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-putin-diesel-deal-not-094000834.html) since the deal was announced.
On the gasoline front, Trump’s only utterances about potentially lower prices are that gas will get cheaper once the [Iran war ends](https://www.facebook.com/kbtxmedia/posts/trump-has-told-reporters-and-supporters-that-gas-prices-will-fall-once-the-war-w/1543566817800122/). That stands to reason, but the price-dropping process will be slow-going once the Strait of Hormuz opens."If and when that happens, it will be a very long, multi-month to multi-year process for things to fully normalize," says a GasBuddy petroleum expert [quoted on CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/iran-war-gas-prices-oil/?utm_source=chatgpt.com).
The economically painful results of Trump’s hapless venture into the Persian Gulf will linger for a long time. The [Center for Strategic and International Studies](https://www.csis.org/analysis/postwar-threat-gulf-energy-infrastructure) sees localized conflicts, many of them stirred up during Trump’s incursion into the area, as a “postwar threat to Gulf energy infrastructure.”
Unclear as Trump’s objectives in this war have been, his [options](https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2026/10/americas-least-bad-option-in-iran.html) seem even more muddled, which is a natural follow-up to the [discordant](https://www.theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/08/trump-foreign-policy-incoherence-iran/688312/) statements and [erratic](https://www.scmp.com/news/world/middle-east/article/3347579/trumps-erratic-strategy-iran-raises-questions-about-us-war-preparation) strategies that got us into this mess in the first place.

item.title: Why artificial intelligence can’t replace your financial planner
item.description:
What is a financial planner worth when anyone can get a plan from ChatGPT? A student asked this question during a recent video call with the Wealth Management Society at Brigham Young University–Idaho. Here is my answer.

AI can already read financial documents, run a tax analysis, and estimate how long retirement savings may last. It is getting good at supplying answers that can help build a sound technical plan. I expect more people to arrive at a planner’s office having done much of that work themselves, so the conversation can start at a higher level.

Yet the logical answers AI gives are of limited value in making money decisions, which are seldom made on logic alone. Stanford marketing professor Baba Shiv has suggested that 90 to 95 percent of our decisions are shaped by emotion without our being aware of it. If money decisions were logical, nobody would overspend, everyone would live within a budget, and every worker would be saving for retirement.

People who are stuck on a money decision usually do not need another answer. They need someone to listen long enough for them to reach their own answer. In my early years as a financial planner, I was the advice and answer man. I couldn’t see why anyone would turn down my logical and correct advice. I learned, painfully, to shut up until it was time to give advice, and then to ask permission first.

For example, a client in my financial therapy practice came in for a recent session stuck on a decision between three options I will call A, B, and C. Almost immediately, I thought B was the answer. Instead of saying so, I got curious and asked questions, and we spent the whole hour looking at what each option meant to her. At the end she said, “I think the answer is B for me.”

I could have given her that answer right away, which is what a chatbot might have done. In my experience, though, people are far more likely to act on an answer they reach themselves than on one someone hands them.

My intent is not to discourage anyone from using AI with their money. I use it to manage my calendar and email and to analyze my financial documents, and I’m often amazed at what it finds.

Here are my suggestions for using AI with your finances:

  • If you are researching a financial decision, use AI as a research tool. I do this before medical appointments. I arrive better informed, and my doctor and I can have a more useful conversation. However, I am not naive enough to act on what AI tells me without first consulting a medical professional.

  • If you are about to make a large or hard-to-reverse decision, such as rolling over a 401(k) or deciding how much you can safely spend in retirement, have a professional look at your situation first. AI offers confident, specific answers that carry no accountability, and it can be right most of the time and still be wrong on a detail that is costly to miss.

  • If you already know what you should do and are not doing it, an AI answer is unlikely to help. Look for a planner or financial therapist who listens and asks questions first, and who asks permission before giving advice.

AI is an evolving tool, not a magic source of instant answers. I strongly recommend that you let AI help do the research. Then bring that research to a professional advisor who will help you find solutions and strategies that are the best fit for you.

item.source:markdown:
What is a financial planner worth when anyone can get a plan from ChatGPT? A student asked this question during a recent video call with the Wealth Management Society at Brigham Young University–Idaho. Here is my answer.
AI can already read financial documents, run a tax analysis, and estimate how long retirement savings may last. It is getting good at supplying answers that can help build a sound technical plan. I expect more people to arrive at a planner’s office having done much of that work themselves, so the conversation can start at a higher level.
Yet the logical answers AI gives are of limited value in making money decisions, which are seldom made on logic alone. Stanford marketing professor Baba Shiv has suggested that [90 to 95 percent of our decisions are shaped by emotion](https://us.list-manage.com/iiD817U_0PS?e=f6092c9c7b&c2id=bb5d24e9334e337e2f8dc8f2d6061031) without our being aware of it. If money decisions were logical, nobody would overspend, everyone would live within a budget, and every worker would be saving for retirement.
People who are stuck on a money decision usually do not need another answer. They need someone to listen long enough for them to reach their own answer. In my early years as a financial planner, I was the advice and answer man. I couldn’t see why anyone would turn down my logical and correct advice. I learned, painfully, to shut up until it was time to give advice, and then to ask permission first.
For example, a client in my financial therapy practice came in for a recent session stuck on a decision between three options I will call A, B, and C. Almost immediately, I thought B was the answer. Instead of saying so, I got curious and asked questions, and we spent the whole hour looking at what each option meant to her. At the end she said, “I think the answer is B for me.”
I could have given her that answer right away, which is what a chatbot might have done. In my experience, though, people are far more likely to act on an answer they reach themselves than on one someone hands them.
My intent is not to discourage anyone from using AI with their money. I use it to manage my calendar and email and to analyze my financial documents, and I’m often amazed at what it finds.
Here are my suggestions for using AI with your finances:
- If you are researching a financial decision, use AI as a research tool. I do this before medical appointments. I arrive better informed, and my doctor and I can have a more useful conversation. However, I am not naive enough to act on what AI tells me without first consulting a medical professional.
- If you are about to make a large or hard-to-reverse decision, such as rolling over a 401(k) or deciding how much you can safely spend in retirement, have a professional look at your situation first. AI offers [confident, specific answers that carry no accountability](https://us.list-manage.com/23fEBrwY6P9?e=f6092c9c7b&c2id=bb5d24e9334e337e2f8dc8f2d6061031), and it can be right most of the time and still be wrong on a detail that is costly to miss.
- If you already know what you should do and are not doing it, an AI answer is unlikely to help. Look for a planner or financial therapist who listens and asks questions first, and who asks permission before giving advice.
AI is an evolving tool, not a magic source of instant answers. I strongly recommend that you let AI help do the research. Then bring that research to a professional advisor who will help you find solutions and strategies that are the best fit for you.

item.title: GDP growth comes at expense of consumer savings
item.description:
Fresh data showed the economy grew faster than expected, at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter. Prices grew too, by 3.6%. Robust consumer spending tends to drive GDP, but the consumer savings rate — an important financial cushion — is falling. In this episode, when will strong topline economic figures catch up to a precarious consumer reality? Plus: Alphabet stock slides after a disappointing earnings report, apple orchards reap the devastating effects of unusual spring weather, and jobless stats misalign with labor market perceptions.

item.title: Remembering labor activist Dolores Huerta
item.description:
Dolores Huerta, an icon of labor rights, women's rights, and civil rights, died yesterday at 96. Huerta co-founded what became the United Farm Workers of America, and, for decades, she led strikes and protests pushing for better conditions for agricultural workers. Today, we have a remembrance. Also in this episode: why the Fed held off on raising interest rates and what a proposed hyperscale data center could mean for residents of a rural Alabama town.

item.description:
BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.

But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.

BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.

item.title: AI infrastructure is making smartphones pricier
item.description:
Consumer electronics and AI data centers need memory chips. But there are only a handful of companies in the world that make them. The surge in demand has caused memory shortages and price spikes for everything, including our all-important smartphones.


Gerrit Schneemann is principal analyst at Counterpoint Research, which recently reported global phone prices have jumped by an average of 15%, and even more in markets where consumers can least afford it.

item.title: The Republican brand has gone from shiny to tarnished to toxic
item.description:
The Republican brand has gone from shiny to tarnished, to full-blown toxic.

Republicans used to be fiscally conservative with taxpayer’s money. They used to shun government mandates/controls over us. Republicans used to be respectful. You know, disagreeing without being disagreeable. Not anymore.

The leader of the Republican Party, President Donald Trump is TOTALLY responsible for making the party toxic.

Personal attacks, insults, mocking, and bullying are now the norm coming from him and his people.

To the toxicity add ignoring Congress and an open disdain for the courts that amounts to lawlessness. Think about his words that alienate our allies. Think about his praise of dictators.

His negative behavior has infected all of us. Civility is disappearing. Frustration, friction, and anger are growing.

Republicans used to be interested in building bridges. Now they only want to build walls with razor wire at the top and bottom.

The Republican-controlled Senate and House of Representatives can’t find the courage to tell Trump to STOP. They either agree with everything or are gutless.

Unless he dies, is impeached, or resigns, we are stuck with Trump and his ilk for two more years. Even if he leaves it is obvious Vice President Vance will continue the toxic behavior.

What can we, the voters, do?

It’s simple, we must vote out those supporting the toxicity, at the national and state level. That includes his followers running in the legislature.

Neither of our South Dakota Senators have publicly stood up to Trump. One of them is on the November ballot. Our current Republican Governor supports Trump and, therefore, his toxicity. Our current Republican Attorney General, who wants to be our next member of Congress, had his picture taken with Trump. Both of them giving the “Thumbs Up,” gesture.

Are all Republican elected officials bad, nasty people?

No. But none of them have publicly criticized or renounced Trump’s toxicity.

The only logical conclusion is that they support it or are gutless.

We can’t let that continue.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired

Personal attacks, insults, mocking, and bullying are now the norm coming from him and his people.
To the toxicity add [ignoring Congress](https://campaignlegal.org/CanTrumpDoThat) and an [open disdain for the courts](https://protectdemocracy.org/work/the-trump-administrations-conflict-with-the-courts-explained/) that amounts to [lawlessness](https://afj.org/article/supreme-court-bends-the-knee-to-trumps-lawlessness/). Think about his words that [alienate](https://danieldrezner.substack.com/p/donald-trump-is-running-out-of-allies) our allies. Think about his [praise of dictators](https://www.aei.org/commentary/trumps-fondness-for-dictators-and-strongmen-is-more-than-just-unsettling/).
His negative behavior has infected all of us. Civility is disappearing. Frustration, friction, and anger are growing.
Republicans used to be interested in building bridges. Now they only want to build walls with razor wire at the top and bottom.
The Republican-controlled Senate and House of Representatives can’t find the courage to tell Trump to STOP. They either agree with everything or are gutless.
Unless he dies, is impeached, or resigns, we are stuck with Trump and his ilk for two more years. Even if he leaves it is obvious Vice President Vance will continue the toxic behavior.
What can we, the voters, do?
It’s simple, we must vote out those supporting the toxicity, at the national and state level. That includes his followers running in the legislature.
Neither of our South Dakota Senators have publicly stood up to Trump. One of them is on the November ballot. Our current Republican Governor supports Trump and, therefore, his toxicity. Our current Republican Attorney General, who wants to be our next member of Congress, had his picture taken with Trump. Both of them giving the “Thumbs Up,” gesture.
Are all Republican elected officials bad, nasty people?
No. But none of them have publicly criticized or renounced Trump’s toxicity.
The only logical conclusion is that they support it or are gutless.
We can’t let that continue.
_Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired_

item.title: Inflation, gas prices make Trump tax cut savings go pffft
item.description:
Yeah, that was "one big beautiful bill,” alright. What those people in the picture above are preening about as President Trump signs the bill is more like one big beautiful bunch of baloney.

Locally, Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds repeatedly crow about how tax cuts created by Donald Trump's “big, beautiful bill,” were supposed to be a cash windfall for working families. Mike Rounds seems particularly infatuated with the notion, as a line about it seems to show up in every one of his televised ads as he seeks re-election.

You can’t blame Rounds – indeed, you can’t blame the entire Republican Party – for bragging on a tax cut that did, indeed, save working families some money.

Trouble is, their crowing stops short of reality: The money saved on taxes has evaporated into an atmosphere of inflated consumer prices. 

After computing tax savings and the effects of inflation on middle-income Americans, the Institute for Taxation and Economic Policy, in a just released report, concludes that “middle-income Americans are losing an average of $1,670 in 2026 overall, accounting for changes in tax policy and increased inflation that has been boosted by tariffs, the Iran war, and the loss of immigrant workers.”

You don’t have to be an economic analyst to know how inflation has hit your family’s bottom line … or to figure out that the Trump administration and its string of ill-conceived policies have been the driving force for higher prices across the board.

As to the political value of Republican braggadocio about Trump’s tax cuts, is it doing any good as the election draws near?  

As a stand-alone issue, maybe. Overall, though, I doubt it. Polls coming in as mid-terms draw near show the GOP is behind, practically across the board. More specifically, last week’s AP poll shows 84% of respondents say that the cost of living is one of their top concerns.

Cory Heidelberger notes in Dakota Free Press that even in deep red South Dakota a majority of poll respondents say that Trump has hurt the economy.

My hunch is that most people, after they hear Republicans crowing about the money saved by the tax cut, quickly remind themselves and each other that, yeah, it meant more money all right, but what about the cost of food and gas eating it all up?  

Followed by a competing, practically reflexive rejoinder like that, the GOP’s boasting about the “big beautiful bill” is a net political liability. In the political card game, inflation trumps the tax cut.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

item.title: Lower those expectations
item.description:
The housing market is a bit chilly right now — new home sales are down, and so are prices. But current homeowners watched their property values grow over the past several years. So when it comes to selling, they’ve got (as Olivia Rodrigo might say) real big expectations. In this episode, the disconnect between need-to-sell homeowners and price-sensitive buyers. Plus: Consumer confidence continues its bumpy journey, durable goods orders are picking up, and we visit Brownsville, Texas, where SpaceX launches are taking over the skies.

item.title: The rise of class warfare … and why the moneyed class is winning
item.description:
The definition of conservative has changed dramatically over the last two decades. For centuries conservatism simply meant resistance to change—a desire to keep things as they are.

This was especially true of those upper classes whose life was better than others. They wished to keep it that way. Progressives desired change in a way that helped the classes not benefitting from the existing system.

This is nothing new as there has always been a level of class warfare in every society.

There are two kinds of class war—economic and social. The struggle was relatively benign in the United States for centuries. Starting with the Emancipation Proclamation the social struggle became more pronounced. It was the southern wing of the Democratic Party that struggled to hold on to its privileges as the class who enjoyed a high social class status.

With the passage of the Civil Rights Act the southern white class lost much of its superior place in southern society. This strongly exacerbated the struggle with respect to race.

Because it was pushed by a Democratic president, LBJ, many southern whites switched to the Republican Party in the 1970s. Over the last half century that racial social war has not gone away, but has been vastly reduced in scope. Meanwhile, the economic struggle expanded. Under Theodore Roosevelt, the Republican Party became fairly progressive, initiating reforms designed to improve the lives of the working classes.

As the Twentieth Century moved forward, progressive initiatives started to shift to the Democratic Party with the New Deal and other progressive actions of Franklin Roosevelt. These lessened the economic class differential.

The struggle was still relatively benign until the 21st century. The emergence of the Tea Party wing of the Republican Party in 2010 saw an escalation in the economic classs struggle. Those who enjoyed a comfortable lifestyle resented their tax dollars being spent on those they deemed less deserving. Over the last two decades this feeling has grown into serious economic class warfare, with Democrats seeking to make the economic classes less separated and Republicans seeking to preserve the status quo and keep their money to themselves.

Over the preceding decades, progressive successes achieved by liberals — Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps and a variety of other programs — helped the lower economic classes enjoy a higher standard of living. However, this was at the expense of the higher income classes who were understandably opposed. There have been constant conservative efforts to reduce Medicaid and food stamps, now called SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) as well as school lunch and other programs.

In South Dakota the struggle has been shown in many actions. Recent examples are:

Sales tax on food. The legislature has had numerous bills to eliminate the sales tax on food. It has always been rejected because it would seriously reduce state revenues and might require a new source of revenue. An income tax has always been verboten. However, increased revenue from internet sales provided an opportunity to eliminate the sales tax on groceries. Even the Republican governor endorsed the idea. It would reduce costs an average of about $300 per year for a family of four. However this would be relatively equal among all economic classes, disproportionately benefiting the poor. The upper economic classes would not benefit proportionately; it was essentially progressive. This was unacceptable to the legislature and the legislature changed the bill to reduce the overall tax rate by 0.3%. This has the effect of giving more tax reduction to those who spend large amounts of money—businesses and high-income people. A person buying a $100,000 car, boat or machine would save $300 on one item alone. The high income classes won the war over the use of the increased internet sales revenue. The lower economic classes lost in this economic war.

Expanding Medicaid. In 2009 The Medicaid program was expanded to allow states to participate with 90% federal funds to expand Medicaid to the working poor who earned too much to qualify for Medicaid but did not have employer provided health insurance. This would have helped tens of thousands of South Dakotans struggling with day to day living. In economic terms only, the Republican legislature should have endorsed a 9:1 ratio—getting nine dollars for every dollar spent. But this money virtually all went to help the lowest income people in the state. The legislature defeated that bill every year. The money would be better spent on “economic development,” meaning making the wealthy even richer. Finally, the people adopted a constitutional amendment requiring the state to participate. The lower income classes won. However, the legislature did not accept this decision by the people. When the administration proposed reductions to federal funding of the program the legislature proposed its own constitutional amendment (Amendment I on the ballot) ending funding if federal funding is ever reduced. Since funding reduction is a certainty by this administration, passing Amendment I would effectively repeal the citizen-passed amendment. If Amendment I passes, the lower income classes will lose again.

Property tax relief. In 2026 the governor proposed a series of property tax relief measures designed to reduce the property tax on owner occupied residences. They all shift property taxes to sales taxes. All of these programs would give the largest tax relief to the highest income classes of people—distinctly regressive. The lower classes lose. Worse yet, the poorest people in the state rent. When the taxes on their apartment increase, their rent increases. They pay higher taxes and also pay the sales tax and get NO benefit. The poorest people in the state are paying increased sales taxes to pay the property taxes of the richest people in the state.

Pure economic class warfare sponsored by our legislature. From a purely practical standpoint, this makes perfect financial sense. Legislators are elected. And in the vast majority of cases, the candidate with the most money in their campaign chest wins the election and candidates must raise large amounts of money. This comes from people with large amounts of money, and their wishes then dominate the discussion of policy issues. Poor people don’t contribute to political campaigns. They can’t buy influence. If I’m a legislator and need to choose whether to support a large campaign contributor or support the poor, screw the poor.

It is also true at the national level. Congress funds trillions of dollars on wars. Those wars produce millions of veterans. While large portion of their war expenditures come back to them from military contractors, virtually none comes back from veterans. As a result, while trillions are spent on wars creating millions of additional veterans, there have been relatively small increases to the VA in support for veterans. Our Defense Department now spends a trillion dollars; the VA a third of that. (the Defense Department has been correctly renamed the War Department since our military hasn’t defended us from a foreign military invasion since 1812. There is a reason we are called veterans of FOREIGN wars!!)

The class conflict between supporting people at the lower end of the economic ladder and supporting money at the upper end seems to have become more exaggerated in recent decades, but has no obvious solution. Both federally and locally, the money class is winning the struggle. Like all political issues the pendulum seems to swing back and forth. For decades, national policy tended to swing toward helping the less fortunate. Nationally it seems to be swinging back. Locally, the chances of swinging back in the foreseeable future seem remote.

John Cunningham of Sioux Falls has spent his career in local government finance, including in Fulton County, Ga., and Atlanta. He has a master of public administration from Harvard and has done consultant work in four foreign countries.

item.title: Only in San Francisco: A picnic about AI's potential risks
item.description:
Urgent concerns about losing control of AI have burst into the national conversation recently after the OpenAI hack of the open-source AI platform Hugging Face, the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic researcher, and other AI insiders sharing alarmingly high p(doom) figures — that is, the probability that AI kills us all.


An event listing for a picnic beckoned people in the AI scene to spend a Sunday afternoon talking about recent calls to slow down the technology.


Dony Christie, a community organizer in the AI safety scene, chose this spot not for the scenery but because it’s between the offices of Anthropic and OpenAI.


“The hope is, why can't people at the labs just meet at a park in between them and work out a deal?” he said. “I have been concerned about existential risks for a long time. Just like, what do I do to save the world?”
item.source:markdown:
Urgent concerns about losing control of AI have burst into the national conversation recently **[after the OpenAI hack of the open-source AI platform Hugging Face](https://www.marketplace.org/episode/2026/09/10/the-hugging-face-hack-shows-what-happens-when-ai-agents-work-together)**, **[the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic researcher](https://www.marketplace.org/episode/2026/09/11/ai-safety-concerns-grow-as-insiders-issue-urgent-warnings)**, and **[other AI insiders sharing alarmingly high p(doom) figures](https://www.latintimes.com/anthropic-insiders-confirm-ai-could-kill-us-theres-no-plan-yet-599897)** — that is, the probability that AI kills us all.
An **[event listing](https://luma.com/dgc4jlbm)** for a picnic beckoned people in the AI scene to spend a Sunday afternoon talking about recent calls to slow down the technology.
Dony Christie, a community organizer in the AI safety scene, chose this spot not for the scenery but because it’s between the offices of Anthropic and OpenAI.
“The hope is, why can't people at the labs just meet at a park in between them and work out a deal?” he said. “I have been concerned about existential risks for a long time. Just like, what do I do to save the world?”

item.title: The latest on trade negotiations with Canada
item.description:
Trump administration officials say they’re making progress in trade negotiations with Canada. Talks have been stalled since August, when President Donald Trump announced 50% tariffs on a range of imports from Canada. Now, with border states hurting and midterm elections around the corner, negotiations appear to be picking up. We hear where things stand. Then, RadioShack — still alive and kicking — is leaning into retro tech ahead of the holiday shopping season.
