item.title: ﻿Memo to Jackley and Rounds voters: You’re actually voting for Trump
item.description:
South Dakotans can often interact directly with our Senators and Representatives.  Most of us have had personal proximity to them and many actually get to converse.

That understood, these two Republican candidates are regarded by most as regular guys, friendly and polite. By all accounts, and from my own personal experience, Mike Rounds and Marty Jackley are not aloof or hard to deal with and really give not much reason to be disliked. Rounds was regarded as a good governor, and Jackley should have had the opportunity, too.  So, South Dakota Republicans have found it mostly easy to vote for them.

However, this year, votes for Rounds and Jackley are not really votes for Rounds and Jackley.
A vote for either man is a vote for Donald Trump.

Trump’s presidency is, in the words of conservative columnist George Will a “cascading absurdity”. His bumbling, profane, “rallies” are a string of blatant lies and insults; every time he speaks in public it is another disgrace. He’s lied so much that newscasts don’t even bother to point it out. If he’s talking, it’s assumed he is lying, even by supporters who make excuses.

No need to list here all the damage Trump has done and continues to do to our democracy, our present, and our futures. It’s self evident more every day as his approval rating dives to historically low levels.

He’s been able to do this as a consequence of the utter corruption and degradation of the Republican Party. The ability to prevail despite all the mistakes and dangerous ignorance depends on the institutional support of the Republican establishment and its donors.

Neither Jackley nor Rounds (who has claimed that he votes with Trump “99% of the time”) has shown they would be anything other than two more silent partners and two more reliable votes for whatever Trump wants to do.  Some weak disagreement, maybe, but do we think either one will really strongly push back?

Come to attention, Republicans!  Your vote is an unavoidable package deal.

If you vote for these two candidates you are voting for:

  • Betraying Ukrainian patriots, in bed with Vladimir Putin.

  • Ruining our relationship with allies around the world, including our next door neighbors Canada and Mexico.

  • Continuing tariffs, raising prices for consumers, lowering prices for soybeans.

  • Pardoning friends and contributors and those who attacked the Capitol.

  • Family business enrichment, leading to a majority of the public’s perceptions of illegal or unethical behavior.

  • Multi trillion dollar deficits.

  • Historically mistaken war on Iran.

As you vote for Rounds and Jackley, you are implicitly voting for a continuation of all that. Nice guys, yes, but your vote really has not much to do with them. Trump is the Republican Party. Anything that enhances the strength of the party enables the actions of Trump.

It’s understandably difficult for a Republican to vote against either of the two candidates. You like them as individuals.  But do you have the integrity and courage to vote against Trump now knowing that neither of them will do so when the nation needs them?

Thank you for paying attention to this matter.

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

item.source:markdown:
South Dakotans can often interact directly with our Senators and Representatives. Most of us have had personal proximity to them and many actually get to converse.
That understood, these two Republican candidates are regarded by most as regular guys, friendly and polite. By all accounts, and from my own personal experience, Mike Rounds and Marty Jackley are not aloof or hard to deal with and really give not much reason to be disliked. Rounds was regarded as a good governor, and Jackley should have had the opportunity, too. So, South Dakota Republicans have found it mostly easy to vote for them.
However, this year, votes for Rounds and Jackley are not really votes for Rounds and Jackley.
A vote for either man is a vote for Donald Trump.
Trump’s presidency is, in the [words of conservative columnist George Will](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/10/21/trump-putin-alignment-joins-his-many-cascading-absurdities/) a “cascading absurdity”. His bumbling, profane, “rallies” are a string of blatant lies and insults; every time he speaks in public it is another disgrace. He’s [lied so much](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_or_misleading_statements_by_Donald_Trump) that newscasts don’t even bother to point it out. If he’s talking, it’s assumed he is lying, even by [supporters who make excuses](https://captimes.com/opinion/paul-fanlund/opinion-why-donald-trump-s-supporters-tolerate-his-lies/article_018d1de1-ae0b-5f06-8922-852b83142a1e.html).
No need to list here all the damage Trump has done and continues to do to our democracy, our present, and our futures. It’s self evident more every day as his [approval rating](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin) dives to historically low levels.
He’s been able to do this as a consequence of the utter corruption and degradation of the Republican Party. The ability to prevail despite all the mistakes and dangerous ignorance depends on the institutional support of the [Republican establishment and its donors](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/04/trump-maga-inc-500-million-republicans-midterm-elections.html).
Neither Jackley nor Rounds (who has claimed that he votes with Trump [“99% of the time”](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2026/01/22/mike-rounds-formally-announces-campaign-for-reelection-to-u-s-senate/)) has shown they would be anything other than two more silent partners and two more reliable votes for whatever Trump wants to do. Some weak disagreement, maybe, but do we think either one will really strongly push back?
Come to attention, Republicans! Your vote is an unavoidable package deal.
If you vote for these two candidates you are voting for:
- [_Betraying Ukrainian patriots_](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/04/trump-maga-inc-500-million-republicans-midterm-elections.html), in bed with Vladimir Putin.
- [_Ruining our relationship_](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/podcasts/compass-points-with-pbs-news/why-some-u-s-allies-view-trumps-america-as-an-unreliable-boyfriend) with allies around the world, including our next door neighbors Canada and Mexico.
- _Continuing tariffs,_ [raising prices for consumers](https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/10/how-fast-do-tariffs-pass-through-into-consumer-prices/), [lowering prices for soybeans](https://ncga.com/stay-informed/media/the-corn-economy/article/2024/10/trade-study-how-potential-new-tariffs-could-impact-u-s-soybeans-and-corn).
- _Pardoning_ [friends and contributors](https://abcnews.com/US/trumps-flurry-pardons-include-campaign-contributors/story?id=122313284) and those who [attacked the Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pardon_of_January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack_defendants).
- Family business [_enrichment_](https://oversightdemocrats.house.gov/trump-family-corruption-tracker) _,_ leading to a [majority of the public’s](https://time.com/article/2026/10/13/most-americans-think-trump-is-profiting-from-the-presidency-illegally-or-unethically-poll-finds/) perceptions of illegal or unethical behavior.
- Multi trillion dollar [deficits](https://www.crfb.org/press-releases/treasury-confirms-2-trillion-deficit-fiscal-year-2026).
- [_Historically mistaken_](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/content-series/the-big-story/a-misguided-war-a-flawed-deal-and-a-dangerous-future-heres-what-to-do-next-on-iran/) war on Iran.
As you vote for Rounds and Jackley, you are implicitly voting for a continuation of all that. Nice guys, yes, but your vote really has not much to do with them. Trump is the Republican Party. Anything that enhances the strength of the party enables the actions of Trump.
It’s understandably difficult for a Republican to vote against either of the two candidates. You like them as individuals. But do you have the integrity and courage to vote against Trump now knowing that neither of them will do so when the nation needs them?
Thank you for paying attention to this matter.
_Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen_

item.title: When ChatGPT writes your obituary
item.description:
Donna Guthrie had obituaries on her mind after her brother passed away in May. She recently celebrated her 80th birthday and started wondering how she might be remembered. So, she asked ChatGPT to write her obituary. It's the topic of today's “Uncanny AI,” our regular segment about our sometimes unsettling experiences with this tech.


Plus, we asked Michelle Huang, a technologist and artist who explores the use of AI for wonder, if this is creepy or healthy.


More on this:

item.title: Major meeting in Sioux Falls Tuesday on proposed hyperscale data center
item.description:
Editor’s note: You can observe the proceedings of the meeting and have an opportunity to speak. It’s set to discuss a proposed data center between Brandon and Sioux Falls on Tuesday, October 27, 7pm, Carnegie Town Hall, 235 W. 10th St. in Sioux Falls.

The issue of data centers has become a hot button, with the right and the left finding common ground. Democrats, Republicans, Independents and all others have coalesced around opposition to having them anywhere near our own communities.

And for good reasons: they suck the local energy sector dry, which will cause our electricity to fluctuate and cost us dearly in our pocketbooks … they do the same with the local water supply, and it’s unclear how much damage to water tables and our private supplies they will cause … they create noise at decibels well above the safety level for human well-being, and that also includes all the nearby wildlife and insects as well … and the profligate amount of diesel fuel they will house threatens our air and the environment with constant and unabated spills and leaks into the Earth.

On October 27, the Sioux Falls Council and the Lincoln County Commissioners will meet jointly to address the issue of data centers, particularly the Gemini Data Center, which is a proposed hyperscale data center on 164 acres between Brandon and Sioux Falls. There were hours of opposition remarks and testimony given to the SF Council this past January, yet the immediate vote in favor of the 500 megawatt Gemini project was 7-0.

Yet now the politicians have realized this has turned into a real issue with huge public opposition, so they’ve established an Oversight Committee to study potential future regulations on data centers and to gather more public input. This is what the October 27 meeting is all about and I suggest you, dear reader, make every effort to be there.

At least one of the public needs to suggest to the politicians that mitigation is the answer for all of us.

1) on the power issue, any data center should have its own wind turbine (or more) and a solar roof and solar farm. These will not suffice on their own but will help mitigate the huge power needs of each data center.

2) on the water issue, a closed loop system should always be employed and all the water used is to be recycled, so as little as possible is taken from the local supply.

3) on the sound pollution issue, a 30-foot fence should be built around the entire data center itself. Such fences have proven to substantially mitigate the sound from interstate highways, so this fence (to include a closed gate) would help mitigate the noise.

4) hundreds of diesel generators are expected for power augmentation purposes. Emission control devices can mitigate the air pollution of these generators, and fuel containment should be treated as part of critical infrastructure planning (for any and all future leaks).

There are many more issues concerning data centers, but these four stand out as the biggest and most critical. These politicians live here, too, and if they do not require these things, do you really think any company would voluntarily pay these expenses? Besides insisting that our local politicians pass regulations such as mentioned here, they should also eschew any thoughts of tax breaks.

The companies behind these centers represent billions of dollars and they fully intend to make a financial killing on these centers.

We cannot stop them, but we can regulate them and force them to mitigate the coming harm to our communities.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

Photo: U.S. Dept. of Energy computing center in California, ca. 2010. Public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. The issue of data centers has become a hot button, with the right and the left finding common ground. Democrats, Republicans, Independents and all others [have coalesced](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/09/22/americans-views-of-data-centers-have-turned-more-negative/) around opposition to having them anywhere near our own communities.
And for good reasons: they suck the local energy sector dry, which will cause our electricity to fluctuate and cost us dearly in our pocketbooks … they do the same with the local water supply, and it’s unclear how much damage to water tables and our private supplies they will cause … they create noise at decibels well above the safety level for human well-being, and that also includes all the nearby wildlife and insects as well … and the profligate amount of diesel fuel they will house threatens our air and the environment with constant and unabated spills and leaks into the Earth.
On October 27, the Sioux Falls Council and the Lincoln County Commissioners will meet jointly to address the issue of data centers, particularly the Gemini Data Center, which is a proposed hyperscale data center on 164 acres between Brandon and Sioux Falls. There were [hours of opposition remarks](https://siouxfalls.business/hyperscale-data-center-gains-rezoning-vote-after-hours-of-opposing-testimony/) and testimony given to the SF Council this past January, yet the immediate vote in favor of the 500 megawatt Gemini project was 7-0.
Yet now the politicians have realized this has turned into a real issue with huge public opposition, so they’ve established an Oversight Committee to study potential [future regulations](https://www.siouxfalls.gov/government/council/reg_oversight_dc) on data centers and to gather more public input. This is what the October 27 meeting is all about and I suggest you, dear reader, make every effort to be there.
At least one of the public needs to suggest to the politicians that mitigation is the answer for all of us.
1) _on the power issue_, any data center should have its [own wind turbine](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/energy-power-supply/the-pros-and-cons-of-wind-power-for-data-center-sustainability) (or more) and a solar roof and solar farm. These will not suffice on their own but will help mitigate the huge power needs of each data center.
2) _on the water issue_, a [closed loop system](https://blog.vantage-dc.com/2026/04/22/cooling-without-the-drain-how-closed-loop-systems-cut-day-to-day-water-use/) should always be employed and all the water used is to be recycled, so as little as possible is taken from the local supply.
3) _on the sound pollution issue_, a 30-foot fence should be built around the entire data center itself. Such fences have proven to substantially mitigate the sound from [interstate highways](https://www.highwayguardrail.org/products/highway-guardrails/highway-noise-barrier.html), so this fence (to include a closed gate) would help mitigate the noise.
4) _hundreds of diesel generators_ are expected for power augmentation purposes. [Emission control devices](https://www.rypos.com/resources/emissions-blog/clearing-the-air/) can mitigate the air pollution of these generators, and [fuel containment](https://www.consolidatedcontainment.com/blogs/containmentcorner/spill-containment-for-data-center-fuel-systems?srsltid=AYCX9vLEBQheMtnY40Lv-ZJSVYhQ4Ve4r6gd7c93gL-nK-aVtKwzch4-) should be treated as part of critical infrastructure planning (for any and all future leaks).
There are [many more issues](https://www.wri.org/insights/us-data-center-growth-impacts) concerning data centers, but these four stand out as the biggest and most critical. These politicians live here, too, and if they do not require these things, do you really think any company would voluntarily pay these expenses? Besides insisting that our local politicians pass regulations such as mentioned here, they should also eschew any thoughts of tax breaks.
The [companies behind these centers](https://www.sunbirddcim.com/infographic/who-owns-worlds-largest-data-centers) represent billions of dollars and they fully intend to make a financial killing on these centers.
We cannot stop them, but we can regulate them and force them to mitigate the coming harm to our communities.
_Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years._

item.title: Media concentration. It's happening nationally and locally
item.description:
The assertion that a strong democracy needs strong newspapers has been a popular cliche for generations. We might want to take the cliche seriously at a time when both our democracy and our independent news media appear to be in jeopardy.

Increasingly, independent newspapers are going out of business or being purchased by oligarchs and TV networks are consolidating into fewer and fewer hands. About 40% of America's newspapers have shut down since the year 2000. With support from the Trump administration, Paramount Skydance purchased Warner Brothers, including CNN, creating an enormous media empire. David Ellison of Skydance installed Bari Weiss, a right-wing influencer, at CBS News, where she has sought to control the content of news stories while many veteran journalists have resigned. Recently, Weiss has insisted that CBS News pursue negative stories on two Democratic U.S. Senate candidates who are running in highly competitive races: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. The recent allegation that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio proved to be utterly false.

Jeff Bezos, the founder and Chair of Amazon, now owns the Washington Post, which has been one of America's most esteemed newspapers for more than a century. Interestingly, the Post cost Bezos less than half of what he paid for his new super yacht. Bezos has steered the newspaper away from its perceived liberal bias, not wanting to irritate President Trump. 

Across the country, investigative journalism is in trouble, and media organizations concentrate their energies, and their dwindling field reporters, on "feel good" human interest stories. When late night TV personalities like Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert chose to interview Talarico, those interviews were not allowed to air on their programs. Interestingly enough, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) abandoned the Fairness Doctrine, which required equal time for both sides of a political controversy, back in 1987. That does not affect the desire of media titans to avoid rocking the boat by giving exposure to politicians they do not like. 

Here in South Dakota, the decline of independent media is obvious. Weekly newspapers in rural communities continue to shut their doors. Lee Enterprises, which owns the Rapid City Journal, had been saddled with debt ever since it purchased the Pulitzer newspaper chain at a time when readership was about to decline sharply. The Journal now comes out just three times a week, and it no longer covers state and local government as diligently as it did in the past. The staff of reporters is stretched mighty thin.

The masthead of the Rapid City Journal now includes a daily reminder that David Hoffmann of the Hoffmann Media Group is now the "majority shareholder" of the corporation. Interestingly, Lee Enterprises recently purchased the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, the Watertown Public Opinion and the Aberdeen American News, giving it a virtual monopoly of major papers in South Dakota similar to the monopoly that it enjoys in Montana. In South Dakota and nationally, there is a diminished news media in fewer hands. Fewer and fewer reporters are watching, and reporting on, our public policy makers. We can continue to hope that our democracy survives.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

Photo: public domain, wikimedia commons

item.title: iPhone Duo's crease is put to the test
item.description:
Apple's long-awaited iPhone Duo launched this week, and everyone has the same question: can you see a crease? Joanna Stern, founder of media company New Things, has been putting it to the test for her newsletter. She's tried apps, phone calls, cameras. But, she really wanted to know if the much-hyped folding phone would stand the test of time. She hired a hardware designer to build a machine that opened and closed the iPhone Duo over and over while she slept — more than 32,000 times. Stern joins joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino on this week’s “Tech Bytes: Week in Review.”


Plus, Elon Musk says there could be a merger between SpaceX and Tesla. And, recent court documents reveal internal warnings about child safety issues were ignored by TikTok executives.


More on this:

item.title: High risk, high rates — where's the reward?
item.description:
Everyday consumers aren’t the only ones contending with rising borrowing costs. Corporations are also subject to those fluctuations — but the rates don’t rise equally across the board. In this episode, why companies with the corporate equivalent of low credit scores are seeing extra-high borrowing costs right now. Also in this episode: Rising crude oil prices spell trouble for sustained inflation, P&G raises sales with “innovation-based pricing,” and independent mechanics struggle to repair newer tech-integrated cars.


Every story has an economic angle. Want some in your inbox? Subscribe to our daily or weekly newsletter.


Marketplace is more than a radio show. Check out our original reporting and financial literacy content at marketplace.org — and consider making an investment in our future.

  • How rising crude oil prices could impact the U.S. and global economy
  • "Innovation-based pricing": new versions of old products at higher prices
  • Rising rates are stressing out the riskiest companies
  • This CPA quit, then did one fun thing every day of her job hunt
  • Has the recipe for Reese's changed? It depends on how you define 'change'
  • Independent garages juggle mechanic shortage and computerized autos

item.title: Tesla now says it needs its own maps for FSD after years of dismissing maps
item.description:
Tesla says it’s building its own maps to fix some of the most common problems with its “Full Self-Driving” system, including reading speed limits, parking, and choosing routes. The company’s head of AI described the effort on Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call.

It’s a notable shift for a company whose CEO spent years arguing that self-driving systems relying on maps are brittle. And it shows Tesla’s fleet is now doing the same job Waymo’s cars do: mapping the roads so the self-driving system knows what it can’t reliably figure out on its own.

Tesla fans argue that Waymo’s approach differs because it creates HD maps with lidar, but ultimately both are creating their own maps; if your argument is that Tesla’s maps are less well-defined and needed for driving for different reasons than Waymo’s, you don’t really have an argument.

more…
item.source:markdown:
![](https://electrek.co/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/11/Tesla-Software-Update-Interior-2.0.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1400)
Tesla says it’s building its own maps to fix some of the most common problems with its “Full Self-Driving” system, including reading speed limits, parking, and choosing routes. The company’s head of AI described the effort on Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call.
It’s a notable shift for a company whose CEO spent years arguing that self-driving systems relying on maps are brittle. And it shows Tesla’s fleet is now doing the same job Waymo’s cars do: mapping the roads so the self-driving system knows what it can’t reliably figure out on its own.
Tesla fans argue that Waymo’s approach differs because it creates HD maps with lidar, but ultimately both are creating their own maps; if your argument is that Tesla’s maps are less well-defined and needed for driving for different reasons than Waymo’s, you don’t really have an argument.

item.title: Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B
item.description:

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

item.title: Behind the screens: What it’s like to interview an AI news agent
item.description:
At Alaska News, you can find stories about the new summer sales tax rate in Juneau, a man ticketed for killing a bull moose out of season and about 20 other hyperlocal items a day.


Much of the coverage is generated by an AI agent called Walter, as in Cronkite, the famous newsman.


Nathaniel Herz, a human executive editor at the local alt weekly the Anchorage Press, wanted to learn more. So, he asked for an interview.

item.title: Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make
item.description:
Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make. Are they going to stick with their now weak party labels or are they going to break ranks?

The U.S. Senate race includes the incumbent, Senator Mike Rounds. His votes have supported the numerous cutbacks in funding which have negatively affected all of us in one way or another. His silence on numerous important issues is beyond concerning. He wants another term.

The Democrats had a candidate who decided to step aside. Lots of reasons and some back stories to that decision.

Then there is the independent Brian Bengs. He has a solid military career. Was a JAG lawyer. He has been a college professor. He is assertive without being obnoxious. He is listening to us. He wants to take what he is hearing and be OUR voice in the Senate.

Here is the math: Democrats have about 130,000 members. Republicans have a little over 300,000. Independents and no party affiliation voters are about 150,000. 20,000 more than Democrats, and about half as many as Republicans.

Most people I listen to want change in Washington. They are tired of the daily/hourly drama. Their ability to pay bills is harder now because of continuing inflation. They are not happy about tariffs and cuts in programs which help us.

If we truly want change in Washington, Democrats will have to vote in large numbers for Bengs. Same for Independents. An important component is Republicans, many of whom are not happy with Rounds, will have to cross the forbidden line.

Pols done by reputable firms show Bengs either slightly ahead or within the “margin of error.”   It is possible an Independent can win this year.

In Nebraska and Idaho, the Independents running for U.S. Senate are both within the “margin of error.”

If Bengs and the other two can win, there will be five Independents in the U.S. Senate. Enough numbers that both parties will have to pay attention to them.

Voting really matters now. More than ever. Remember in the race for Mayor of Sioux Falls this summer, only FOUR votes separated the top two candidates.

I am optimistic that positive change is coming to Washington. It would be wonderful if South Dakota, you and I are part it.

So, to my diehard Democrat friends, hold your nose if you must and vote for change. To my Republican friends, we are in this mess because of leaders in what used to be a proud, honest, compassionate party. You may need to hold your nose too, and vote for change.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired

item.title: Small town economics clash with Big Tech agendas
item.description:
In Crook County, Oregon, just east of the Cascade mountains, data centers sprawl across the high desert landscape. The area fell into economic decline during the Great Recession and some residents welcomed investment by Meta and Apple in the form of massive data center complexes. But 15 years on, was it worth it? In this episode, what happens when data centers come to town. Plus, mergers and spinoffs: Abbott plans to turn its baby formula operation into a standalone company, and Elon Musk explores a plan to combine Tesla and SpaceX.

item.title: Tesla FSD ‘subscriptions’ hit 1.74M, counted the way Musk’s pay package wants
item.description:
Tesla says it now has 1.74 million active “Full Self-Driving” subscriptions, up 67% from a year ago. A footnote in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter explains how it gets there: the metric follows “our 2025 CEO Performance Award” and “includes both upfront payment and monthly subscriptions.”

So owners who bought FSD outright, some of them years ago, count as subscribers. That matters because 10 million active FSD subscriptions is one of the milestones Elon Musk has to hit to earn his 2025 pay package. It also matters because hundred of thousands of those FSD “subscribers” were sold unsupervised self-driving, which Tesla has yet to deliver.

item.title: Housing affordability, then and now
item.description:
The housing industry got a heap of bad news on Tuesday. New construction was down, and pending home sales dropped to their lowest level since 2001. Higher mortgage interest rates are to blame. The average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate loan is just shy of 7.5%. Average mortgage rates in the '70s were higher, though, and didn't lead to a housing affordability crisis like today's. What gives? And later: lessons from a San Francisco Bay Area universal basic income program.

item.title: ‘Anti-socialist’ Trump announces an $8 billion bailout for farmers.
item.description:
Scrambling for votes at a Kansas Republican pep party last night, President Trump pledged that USDA will be making $8 billion in direct cash payments to American farmers. Combined with the $40 billion he’s already shelled out over the course of his two terms, Trump has given $48 billion in cash to farmers.

Much as I support cash assistance to American farmers – a stable ag economy is probably the  cornerstone of food and national security – this business of Trump financially harming our country’s ag sector with his counter-productive tariffs and inflation-driving foreign policies is getting old and expensive.

As to yesterday’s announcement, farmers shouldn’t be overly enthused about it. Scott Lincicome, VP of General Economics at the Cato Institute calls it “a band-aid on a flesh wound,” adding that at four thousand dollars a farm, “it might cover a few weeks of diesel costs.” As with other announcements (specifically, Russian diesel and imported ground beef) in recent months, Trump is fond of throwing out headline numbers that sound impressive but in actuality don’t do much in the way of helping farmers out with their double economic whammy of low crop prices and high input costs.

More generally, Trump’s reflexive need to look like he’s doing something substantive for producers and consumers has the unexpected political consequence of defining him as that word that he abhors — a socialist.

Disagree? If you consider socialism to be a system where the government intervenes in free market processes by altering free market outcomes, then Trump’s bailout is de facto socialism.

He has said “our country will never be a socialist country,” but, as with many of his other utterances, the president’s rhetoric often contradicts the president's reality.

Paying off farmers for financial troubles created by Trump’s flawed policies has been a recurring theme through both of his terms. He may hate the term, but when he needs to be, Trump is a socialist.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Scrambling for votes at a Kansas Republican pep party last night, [President Trump pledged](https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/trump-plans-8-billion-in-payments-to-farmers-1cec5851) that USDA will be making $8 billion in direct cash payments to American farmers. Combined with the [$40 billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_administration_farmer_bailouts) he’s already shelled out over the course of his two terms, Trump has given $48 billion in cash to farmers.
Much as I support cash assistance to American farmers – a stable ag economy is probably the cornerstone of food and national security – this business of Trump financially harming our country’s ag sector with his [counter-productive tariffs](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/06/trump-trade-war-farmers-warning-signs-00804804) and [inflation-driving foreign policies](https://www.aei.org/commentary/where-is-donald-trumps-affordability-agenda/) is getting old and expensive.
As to yesterday’s announcement, farmers shouldn’t be overly enthused about it. [Scott Lincicome](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/06/trump-trade-war-farmers-warning-signs-00804804), VP of General Economics at the Cato Institute calls it “a band-aid on a flesh wound,” adding that at four thousand dollars a farm, “it might cover a few weeks of diesel costs.” As with [other announcements](https://www.sdstandardnow.com/home/trumps-deal-on-russian-diesel-fuel-isnt-likely-to-lower-fuel-prices-for-farmers) (specifically, Russian diesel and imported ground beef) in [recent months](https://farmpolicynews.illinois.edu/2026/10/trump-import-plan-bringing-in-less-affordable-beef-than-allowed/), Trump is fond of throwing out headline numbers that sound impressive but in actuality don’t do much in the way of helping farmers out with their double economic whammy of [low crop prices](https://tradingeconomics.com/commodity/corn) and [high input costs](https://www.fb.org/intel/markets/production-costs-expected-to-reach-new-highs-in-2027).
More generally, Trump’s reflexive need to look like he’s doing something substantive for producers and consumers has the unexpected political consequence of [defining him](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/donald-trump-most-powerful-socialist-154604027.html) as that word that he abhors — a socialist.
Disagree? If you consider socialism to be a system where the government intervenes in free market processes by altering free market outcomes, then Trump’s bailout is _de facto_ socialism.
[He has said](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefings-statements/remarks-president-trump-state-union-address-2/) “our country will never be a socialist country,” but, as with many of his other [utterances](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/08/us/politics/trump-third-term-gaza-contradictions.html#:~:text=Trump%20has%20used%20a%20dizzying,sometimes%20in%20the%20same%20day.), the president’s rhetoric often contradicts the president's reality.
Paying off farmers for [financial troubles created](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_administration_farmer_bailouts) by Trump’s flawed policies has been a recurring theme through both of his terms. He may hate the term, but when he needs to be, Trump is a socialist.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Bumble didn't find its match on the stock market
item.description:
When Bumble went public five years ago, the dating app known for being a friendlier place for women was valued at $14 billion. But the dating business, the tech industry and the stock market have changed a lot since then. And shares declined 90% from their peak.


Now, the company is going private again. It's being acquired by private equity firm Ithaca Holdings, with two new CEOs taking the helm. Sarah Kunst, managing director at the venture firm Cleo Capital and former senior advisor at Bumble, explains what this all means.


More on this:


“Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'“ from BBC


“Here's what happens to Twitter's stock now that it's a private company” from NBC News


“EA is now a private company” from The Verge

item.title: Polestar and Oxford wired up drivers to measure how performance feels
item.description:
Polestar and the University of Oxford put 12 drivers in eye trackers and heart-rate monitors and sent them around a Swedish racetrack in two versions of the Polestar 4. The goal was to put numbers on something no spec sheet captures: how performance feels to the person driving.

The 544 hp Polestar 4 Dual motor with Performance pack delivered 32% higher peak acceleration than the 268 hp Rear motor version on matched laps, and it needed 15% less steering effort to do it. Drivers also rated it far higher on the experience.

more…
item.source:markdown:
![](https://electrek.co/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/10/polestar-oxford-performance-study-hero.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1333)
Polestar and the University of Oxford put 12 drivers in eye trackers and heart-rate monitors and sent them around a Swedish racetrack in two versions of the Polestar 4. The goal was to put numbers on something no spec sheet captures: how performance feels to the person driving.
The 544 hp Polestar 4 Dual motor with Performance pack delivered 32% higher peak acceleration than the 268 hp Rear motor version on matched laps, and it needed 15% less steering effort to do it. Drivers also rated it far higher on the experience.

item.title: The hidden costs of artificial intelligence: Are you paying attention?
item.description:
According to an August 2026 article in Business Insider, a Microsoft employee ran up $28,000 in artificial intelligence charges in 28 days without buying anything.

He was using AI tools to do his job, and the company was billed for what the industry calls tokens. A token is a small unit of work: you ask one of these systems a question, it breaks the question into pieces and works through them, and each piece is a billable token.

AI tokens make up a new kind of business expense that companies are beginning to budget for. Individual users will eventually see this cost, too, even though most AI tools are still free or nearly free.

I recently encountered this myself when I hit a usage limit on an AI tool in the middle of a project. Not wanting to wait five hours for the allowance to reset, I told it to bill me for the overage. It only took 15 minutes to burn through nearly $50. Because I had notifications turned on, I could see the meter running and shut down the program.

Without that real-time notification, I might have gone merrily on my way until I finished my project, then been shocked when I realized what it had cost. This may well be what happened for the Microsoft employee who ran up the headline-worthy tab.

Tokens, like subscriptions and utility bills, are metered money. If I buy a five-dollar cup of coffee and swipe a card or hand over cash, I actively participate in the transaction. Metered money, by contrast, runs up in the background. We tend not to notice it because we are not deliberately deciding to spend it in the moment.

If you are among the many people beginning to use AI tools, be aware that at some point you will need to budget for them. Here are few ideas to help you avoid expensive surprises.

Be aware that paid AI services are likely to follow the same patterns as other metered services. A subscription model is a series of small yeses. This app or that service seems worth trying out for a small amount. Then, even if we don’t continue to use it, it keeps renewing until we notice that we’re paying for something we’ve forgotten to cancel. These systems are built so that paying takes no effort, which is exactly why the charges go unnoticed.

The pattern especially worth watching is the free tier that turns into a paid one. Metered services often start out free or at a low cost. The price then increases once you have built the habit of using the service.

Token billing will be even harder to plan for than subscriptions, because it is not a fixed or predictable monthly amount. It moves with how much the tool gets used, which makes it easy to underestimate.

If you are a fan of AI, how can you use it and also protect your budget? First, research any tools you might use so you understand the potential charges. Then set a number now for what these tools are worth to you in a month. Put any metered charges on one card, so you’ll have a monthly total you can see.

Budgeting in advance means making an active, deliberate decision. If you wait for the statement and react, you are passing judgment on yourself after the fact. This rarely changes what anyone does the next month.

For many people, AI tools will be worth paying for. However, it is wise to decide, before any bills arrive, how much in very real money those tools are worth to you.

item.title: Consumer credit creep
item.description:
Inflation is affecting all of us. But when costs go up, lower-income households are especially vulnerable to credit creep — that’s when consumers use credit for more and more transactions. One survey found 29% of buy now, pay later users took out the loans to pay for groceries, double the percentage from just a couple of years ago. Also in this episode: What might happen to the labor market if Fed raises interest rates, how immigration crackdowns are tied to a 14-year homebuilder confidence low, and why political candidates are competing for AI attention.

item.title: Tesla (TSLA) proxy shows a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger
item.description:
Tesla’s proxy for its 2026 annual meeting, filed today, confirms that one of its supposedly independent directors now sits on SpaceX’s board. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both Tesla’s compensation committee and its governance committee, joined SpaceX’s board in February.

That’s one of several details in the filing that line up with a Tesla-SpaceX merger. There’s a three-item ballot, an auto-voting program that kicks in for the next vote, and Musk pay terms that pay out on a deal price alone.

item.title: What exactly is the just-launched Vote Independent Movement?
item.description:
What exactly is the Vote Independent Movement?

I have been an independent my entire adult life.

Not because I believe Democrats and Republicans are the same. They aren’t. Not because I split my vote evenly between them. I don’t. And not because I think “independent” is another word for moderate.

Mostly, I’ve stayed independent because my beliefs have never fit neatly enough inside a political party to hand one my loyalty in advance.

That distinction has become unexpectedly relevant to my work.

This week, independent U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs launched the Vote Independent Movement, or VIM, a new project built around a two-sentence pledge: I pledge to consider every problem based on objective facts. I am not and will not be bound to automatically support the platform of, or the leaders of, any political party.

Brian founded it. I serve as its director.

So what exactly is it? For now, the simplest answer is the most accurate one: VIM is a movement built around a pledge, not a new political party.

That’s it.

There is no requirement to change your voter registration. A Republican can take it and remain a Republican. A Democrat can take it and remain a Democrat. An independent can take it without committing to vote for independent candidates.

And, importantly, taking the pledge does not commit someone to voting for Brian Bengs.

That last point is worth explaining because VIM’s origin is unusual.

Brian created the movement during his campaign for U.S. Senate, and VIM is currently a project of the Bengs campaign, paid for by the campaign.

Bengs says the idea grew out of his experience campaigning across South Dakota and repeatedly encountering people frustrated by the expectation that supporting a political party also requires automatically supporting its leaders and positions.

That experience led to a broader question: Is political independence primarily a voter-registration category, or can it describe a way of approaching politics?

The numbers make the question interesting.

Gallup reported in January that a record 45% of U.S. adults identified politically as independents in 2025, compared with 27% each identifying as Republicans and Democrats.

In South Dakota, 156,908 of 626,871 active registered voters are Independent or No Party Affiliation, more than the number registered as Democrats.

But those numbers have limits.

They don’t tell us why someone registered without a party. They don’t mean 45% of Americans share a political philosophy. And they certainly don’t mean those people agree with one another.

In some ways, that’s the more interesting part.

VIM isn’t attempting to create a platform that all those people agree on. The pledge doesn’t say what to believe about abortion, immigration, taxes, guns, health care, war or data centers. Two people could take it, examine the same issue honestly, and reach completely different conclusions.

The agreement is about the process: evidence first, conclusion second. Party label doesn’t settle the question.

The premise is that this matters most when the problems are hard. From the cost of living and rural health care to Social Security and trillion-dollar deficits, our country isn’t short on problems whose solutions demand serious choices. VIM’s argument is simply that party loyalty shouldn’t determine the answer before the facts do.

There is another question we deliberately haven’t answered yet: What does VIM become after Election Day?

We don’t know.

The website says so plainly. It could remain a movement, become an organization or take another form. The immediate experiment is much narrower: put the pledge in front of people, count how many take it, and see whether the idea has life beyond the campaign that produced it.

That uncertainty is real, not coyness.

I’ve spent much of the past year working in South Dakota politics and creating spaces where people with very different political beliefs can actually hear one another. One thing I’ve learned is that “independent” is an imprecise word. It can describe a registration, an ideology, a temperament, a protest against the two-party system or simply a person who doesn’t want a label.

VIM is testing another definition.

Independent can be a verb.

Look at the facts. Question your own side. Allow yourself to change your mind. Then decide.

Whether enough people find meaning in that definition to build something lasting around it is the part we don’t know yet.

And that’s probably the most interesting part of the experiment.

Ngoc Thach lives in South Dakota and is the director of the Vote Independent Movement

item.title: Should voters let chatbots do their election homework?
item.description:
Are you doing your homework ahead of the midterms or just planning to wing it at the ballot box? While you may have a good idea already about who you want for House, Senate, or governor, there’s still other studying to do before Election Day. But in 2026, the word “homework” often means “ask an AI-powered chatbot.” For voters, that’s both a resource and a risk. First though: why economic uncertainty is translating into a flood of imports.

item.title: Using generative AI for election-related research
item.description:
You might say the 2026 midterms are the first big AI election. The technology has become a key political issue, it’s a significant source of fundraising and it’s also helping power campaign ads.


Plus, generative AI is being looked to by voters as a tool for sorting through the deluge of information, especially in places like California where there are 14 ballot propositions to research.


Marketplace's senior correspondent for Future Effects, David Brancaccio, put three AI chatbots to the test.


More on this:


“Electoral Hallucinations: Safeguarding UK elections in the world of LLMs and AI chatbots” from Demos


“AI chatbots can effectively sway voters – in either direction” from Cornell Chronicle
